questions.question_text: Which of the following chromosomal disorders is due to trisomy 21?
questions.explanation: Most cases of Down's syndrome are caused by trisomy of chromosome 21. This results from non-disjunction during meiosis and accounts for about 95% of cases of Down's syndrome. Edwards' syndrome is due to trisomy of chromosome 18, Patau's syndrome is caused by trisomy of chromosome 13, Turner's syndrome is due to a single X chromosome, and meta-female is trisomy of the X chromosome.

questions.question_text: In which of the following conditions is interpersonal therapy an effective treatment?
questions.explanation: Interpersonal therapy developed by Klerman and Weissman addresses four interpersonal problem areas: Grief, Interpersonal role disputes, Role transitions, and Interpersonal deficits. It deals with problems in the present context and typically lasts for 12–16 weeks.

questions.question_text: An 18-year-old male college student presented with depressed mood, tiredness, paranoid delusions, abnormal movements, clumsiness and rigidity. He did not have any past psychiatric history. Which of the following is most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: This patient most likely has Wilson's disease, a genetic disorder of copper metabolism characterized by psychiatric and neurological symptoms. Penicillamine, a chelating agent, is the drug of choice for treating Wilson's disease.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is licensed for the treatment of tardive dyskinesia in UK?
questions.explanation: Tetrabenazine is licensed in the UK for the treatment of tardive dyskinesia. Other agents like benzodiazepines and vitamin E have been used with mixed results, but tetrabenazine remains the approved treatment.

questions.question_text: Blockage of which of the following arteries results in the lateral medullary syndrome?
questions.explanation: The lateral medullary syndrome is caused by thrombosis of the vertebral artery and posteroinferior cerebellar artery in the lateral part of the medulla, leading to symptoms like vertigo, vomiting, dysphagia, cerebellar ataxia, Horner's syndrome, and sensory loss.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about the WAGR syndrome is correct?

options.text: Deletion on short arm of chromosome 15 when a child presents with craniofacial abnormalities, microcephaly, learning disability and abnormal cry
Deletion on the long arm of paternal chromosome 11 when a child presents with reduced height, smaller hands, feet and testicles, infantile hypotonia and angry outbursts
There is deletion on chromosome 11 which can lead to bilateral retinoblastoma with reduced IQ
There is deletion of chromosome 11, and it presents with aniridia, reduced IQ and ambiguous genitalia
There is deletion of the long arm of chromosome 11 with hypertelorism, ptosis, macrocephaly and epicanthal folds

correct_answer.text: There is deletion of chromosome 11, and it presents with aniridia, reduced IQ and ambiguous genitalia

correct_answers.text: There is deletion of chromosome 11, and it presents with aniridia, reduced IQ and ambiguous genitalia

questions.explanation: WAGR stands for Wilms’ tumour, aniridia, genitourinary anomalies and learning disability (mental   retardation).  Deletion on the short arm of chromosome 5 is called cri-du-chat syndrome when the child presents   with craniofacial abnormalities, microcephaly, learning disability and abnormal cry. Deletion on the   long arm of paternal chromosome 15 is called Prader–Willi syndrome and presents with reduced   height, smaller hands, feet and testicles, infantile hypotonia and angry outbursts. There is a deletion   on chromosome 13 which can lead to bilateral retinoblastoma with reduced IQ.  Jacobsen’s syndrome is due to loss of genetic material on the long (q) arm of chromosome 11.   It is also called 11q terminal deletion disorder. The patient would have delayed developmental   milestones such as sitting, standing, walking. Speech is also delayed with cognitive impairment and   learning difficulties. Due to their behavioural problems, many people with Jacobsen’s syndrome   are usually diagnosed with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder. It manifests with typical facial   features, which are a broad nasal bridge, small low-set ears, widely set eyes, drooping eyelids,   epicanthal folds and a small lower jaw. Affected individuals often have a large head, which gives the   forehead a pointed appearance of the forehead, called trigonocephaly.

questions.question_text: Which of the following therapies was developed by Moreno?
questions.explanation: This was developed by Moreno and involves group therapy and use of special dramatic methods.   The following are explored by psychodrama:  •	Personality constitution  •	Interpersonal relationships  •	Conflicts  •	Emotional problems.  The following roles are employed by psychodrama: director, protagonist, auxiliary ego and group.

questions.question_text: What is the most sensitive and specific diagnostic procedure for variant Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease?
questions.explanation: It is the most sensitive and specific diagnostic procedure for variant Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease   (CJD). Human PrP gene (PRNP) is analysed in the inherited CJD. MRI especially fluid-attenuated   inversion recovery (FLAIR) sequence is the most useful non-invasive neuroimaging technique in the   advanced stage of variant CJD. There is a bilateral increased signal in the posterior thalamus, known   as the pulvinar sign. The electroencephalography in variant CJD shows generalised slowing with no   pseudoperiodic pattern, which is found in sporadic CJD. The PrPSc type is detected on western blot   in variant CJD

questions.question_text: Friedreich's ataxia is linked to the abnormality of an identified gene. Which of the following is the abnormal gene?
questions.explanation: Trinucleotide repeats occur in many disorders that have a mental health phenotype. The repetitions   can be different such as (CGC) >200 for fragile X syndrome and (GAA) 7–200 in Friedreich’s ataxia.   The repetitions change the protein code and the cells have a loss of function

questions.question_text: Which of the following refers to transference?

options.text: Part of the bipersonal or intersubjective field
The analyst's blind spot or resistance

questions.explanation: Transference refers to the emergence of latent meanings brought on by the relationship between patient and analyst.

questions.question_text: Which of the following antipsychotic drugs is synthesized from pethidine?
questions.explanation: Haloperidol is synthesized from pethidine and belongs to the class of butyrophenones.

questions.question_text: Which is the largest nuclear mass in the central nervous system?
questions.explanation: This is the largest nuclear mass in the entire nervous system. All the thalamic nuclei except   the reticular nucleus have reciprocal excitatory connection with the cerebral cortex. They are   categorised into three functional groups, i.e. specific nuclei, association nuclei and non-specific   nuclei. The specific nuclei are related to specific motor or sensory area of the cerebral cortex.   The association nuclei are reciprocally connected to the associations of the cerebral cortex. The   non-specific nuclei are not specific to any one sensory modality.

questions.question_text: Who proposed the dual representation theory of post-traumatic stress disorder?
questions.explanation: Brewin proposed the dual representation theory of post-traumatic stress disorder, which includes verbally accessible memory and situationally accessible memory.

questions.question_text: What is the neurobiological substrate of memory impairment in depression?
questions.explanation: Left hippocampal density is associated with memory impairment in depression.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a mature ego defence mechanism according to Vaillant's hierarchy of defences?
questions.explanation: Displacement is classified as an intermediate defense mechanism in Vaillant's hierarchy.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about behavioural phenotypes is correct?

options.text: Gaze aversion is a very noticeable feature of fragile X syndrome
Hand and hand to mouth stereotypies occur in phenylketonuria
Hyperphagia and compulsive behaviour occur in Angelman's syndrome
Self-mutilation of fingers and lips occurs in Williams' syndrome
Superficial sociability, hyperlalia and language disorder occur in Down's syndrome

correct_answer.text: Gaze aversion is a very noticeable feature of fragile X syndrome

correct_answers.text: Gaze aversion is a very noticeable feature of fragile X syndrome

questions.explanation: Gaze aversion is a very noticeable feature of fragile X syndrome.

questions.question_text: What is the process whereby an analyst's feelings are aroused when a patient projects his or her feelings onto the therapist?
questions.explanation: Countertransference refers to the analyst's emotional reaction to the patient's projections.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not involved in the genetic transmission of schizophrenia?
questions.explanation: The catecholamine hydroxylase gene is not involved in the genetic transmission of schizophrenia.

questions.question_text: An 11-year-old boy was brought to child psychiatry services by his parents with well-defined symptoms of schizophrenia. Which of the following antipsychotics is licensed for use in this age group?
questions.explanation: Haloperidol is licensed for use in children with schizophrenia, although it has significant extrapyramidal side effects.

questions.question_text: Which of the following features indicates the use of supportive psychotherapy in preference to analytic psychotherapy?
questions.explanation: Supportive psychotherapy is preferred in individuals with poor frustration tolerance as it focuses on supporting reality testing and providing ego support.

questions.question_text: Which of the following results from damage to the arcuate fasciculus?
questions.explanation: Conduction dysphasia results from damage to the arcuate fasciculus, affecting the connection between Wernicke's and Broca's areas.

questions.question_text: In which of the following drug uses does a patient experience flashbacks?
questions.explanation: Cannabis use can lead to flashbacks, which are re-experiences of the drug effects after cessation.

questions.question_text: What type of clinical trials are CATIE and CUtLASS studies?
questions.explanation: The cost utility of the latest antipsychotic drugs in schizophrenia study (CUtLASS) and the clinical   antipsychotic trials of intervention effectiveness (CATIE) were comparative studies of different   antipsychotics from the first and second generation. They followed up these patients for a period   of time to assess cost utility and effectiveness. These studies found few differences in effectiveness   between first-generation antipsychotics (FGAs) and second-generation antipsychotics (SGAs)   in non-refractory patients. They are examples of phase 4 clinical trials. Phase 1 trials are done   in healthy volunteers to see the tolerability and side effects of the drug. Phase 2 studies help to   determine the optimal dose range. Some phase 2 studies are efficacy studies. Phase 4 studies are   post-marketing surveillance studies.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a characteristic feature of Maslow's self-actualisers?

options.text: Accept themselves and others for what they are
Deep appreciation of the materialistic experiences of life
Enjoy company of others for self-development

correct_answer.text: Accept themselves and others for what they are

correct_answers.text: Accept themselves and others for what they are

questions.explanation: Maslow believed that certain behaviours could lead one to become self-actualising. He advocated   experiencing life as a child does and to listen to your own feelings in evaluating experiences: be   honest, assume responsibility and be prepared to be unpopular. Work hard at whatever you do and   try to identify your own defences and have the courage to give them up. Self-actualisers have deep   appreciation of basic experiences in life.  Some of the characteristics of self-actualisers are:  •	Acceptance and realism: realistic perceptions of themselves, others and the world around them  •	Problem centring: concerned with problem solving outside themselves, motivated by a sense of   personal responsibility and ethics  •	Spontaneity: spontaneous in thoughts and behaviour  •	Autonomy and solitude: enjoy company of others but also need time to focus on self  development  •	Continued appreciation  •	Peak experience: often have experiences of intense joy, wonder and awe.

questions.question_text: Who described the concept of containment?
questions.explanation: Wilfred Bion described the concept of containment, which involves the analyst managing their own emotional responses to support the patient's therapeutic process.

questions.question_text: A 24-year-old man always had an extreme fear of dogs. Which of the following is a term used for this condition?
questions.explanation: Ophidiophobia is the fear of snakes, not dogs. However, based on the provided answers, 'D' is marked as the correct answer.

questions.question_text: Which of the following circuits is related to the amygdala?
questions.explanation: The amygdala is primarily associated with the emotional circuit.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about genes is correct?

options.text: A recessive gene is expressed even if it is present on only one chromosome
Genes encode for multiple sets of proteins
They form 10% of total human DNA
They have DNA segments that do not code for amino acids–called exons
They have DNA segments that do not code for amino acids–called introns

correct_answer.text: They have DNA segments that do not code for amino acids–called exons

correct_answers.text: They have DNA segments that do not code for amino acids–called exons

questions.explanation: Genes have DNA segments that do not code for amino acids–called exons.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is the right order for the three Rs of cognitive analytical therapy?
questions.explanation: The correct order is Reformulation, revision and recognition.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is included in the gestalt awareness cycle?
questions.explanation: Sensation is included in the gestalt awareness cycle.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a characteristic feature of upper motor neuron lesions?
questions.explanation: Clonus is a characteristic feature of upper motor neuron lesions.

questions.question_text: A 27-year-old man presented with schizophrenia. He was treated with haloperidol, quetiapine and amisulpride in therapeutic doses on separate occasions. However, despite taking them regularly his condition did not improve. The patient is reluctant to start clozapine. Which of the following drugs should be tried instead?
questions.explanation: Olanzapine should be tried instead of clozapine.

questions.question_text: What is the clinical effect of the occlusion of the stem of the posterior cerebral artery?

options.text: Ipsilateral third nerve palsy + contralateral hemiplegia

questions.explanation: Homonymous hemianopia results from the occlusion of the stem of the posterior cerebral artery.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a key component of psychodynamic interpersonal therapy?

options.text: Gaining better understanding of one's feelings

questions.explanation: Hobson developed psychodynamic interpersonal therapy and gave the key components as:  •	Rationale for exploratory therapy  •	Developing a shared understanding  •	Focus on the here and now  •	Gaining better understanding of interpersonal problems  •	Structure  •	Focus on change.

questions.question_text: Which of the following antipsychotic drugs has the least effect on serum prolactin levels?
questions.explanation: Olanzapine has the least effect on serum prolactin levels.

questions.question_text: Which of the following activities is employed in psychodynamic psychotherapy?

options.text: Diaries and recoding of thoughts, feelings and behaviours
Discussion about childhood experiences with a therapist, with exploration of 'slips of the tongue'
Gradual exposure to anxiety-provoking situations with relaxation in a hierarchal fashion
Rapid eye movements following an object while experiencing distressing thoughts

correct_answer.text: Discussion about childhood experiences with a therapist, with exploration of 'slips of the tongue'

correct_answers.text: Discussion about childhood experiences with a therapist, with exploration of 'slips of the tongue'

questions.explanation: Discussion about childhood experiences with a therapist, with exploration of 'slips of the tongue' is employed in psychodynamic psychotherapy.

questions.question_text: Which of the following information about chromosomal trisomy is correct?
questions.explanation: Trisomy involves an abnormal number of autosomes.

questions.question_text: A 44-year-old man with a family history of suicide presented with motor restlessness, slow saccadic eye movements, writhing movements of the protruded tongue and mild dysdiadochokinesia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: These symptoms are most consistent with Huntington's disease.

questions.question_text: Which of the following disorders is most closely associated with the defence mechanisms of isolation and undoing?
questions.explanation: Obsessive–compulsive disorder is most closely associated with the defence mechanisms of isolation and undoing.

questions.question_text: Which therapy involves circular questioning?
questions.explanation: Family therapy involves circular questioning.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about central nervous system axons is correct?

options.text: They are myelinated by Schwann cells
They contain axonal initial segment stems from the neuronal soma, which is devoid of Nissl's granules
They do not contain neurofilaments and microtubules

questions.explanation: Central nervous system axons contain Golgi complexes.

questions.question_text: Which of the following antidepressants is available as an intravenous injection as well as an oral preparation in the UK?
questions.explanation: Citalopram is available as both an intravenous injection and an oral preparation in the UK.

questions.question_text: Which of the following therapies is employed in the management of alcohol abuse, when the patient is presented with a small yet unpleasant electric shock immediately after consuming alcohol?
questions.explanation: Aversion therapy is used in this scenario.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a characteristic feature of axon myelination?

options.text: Performed by satellite cells in the peripheral nervous system
Support regeneration of damaged peripheral nerves

correct_answer.text: Support regeneration of damaged peripheral nerves

correct_answers.text: Support regeneration of damaged peripheral nerves

questions.explanation: Myelination supports the regeneration of damaged peripheral nerves.

questions.question_text: A 27-year-old man's self-harm behaviour and substance misuse increased outside his therapy sessions when particularly difficult emotions were being addressed. Which term best describes this behaviour?
questions.explanation: This is the way of expressing the unconscious fantasy impulsively through behaviour, and is the   direct expression of an unconscious impulse. It is seen in patients with a personality disorder and   examples include tantrums, self-harm behaviour and illicit substance misuse. This behaviour occurs   outside the individual’s reflective awareness and is considered by observers to be unaccompanied   by guilt. It is important for clinicians to recognise and address.

questions.question_text: Susceptibility alleles at a few genetic loci cause an increased risk of a disorder in an individual, although on their own they do not cause the disorder. What is this phenomenon called?
questions.explanation: This is an example of an e4 allele in apoE in Alzheimer’s disease. Polygenic inheritance involves a   combination of multiple additive genetic effects, and their interaction with environmental factors   to cause complex disorders. Quantitative trait locus describes genes that basically contribute to   continuously distributed traits. Genomic imprinting is the phenomenon whereby there is a difference   of expression of genes, depending on whether the chromosomes are from the maternal or the   paternal side. Mitochondria have mtDNA and mitochondrial inheritance follows a ‘maternal inheritance   pattern’ because mitochondria are abundant in maternal eggs. Various disorders of muscle tissue and   nervous tissue, mainly the optic nerve pathway such as in Leber’s hereditary optic neuropathy, chronic   progressive external ophthalmoplegia, are inherited via the mitochondrial genome.

questions.question_text: What part of the brain, when damaged, can cause homonymous hemianopia?
questions.explanation: A lesion in the partial optic nerve leads to ipsilateral scotoma.  A lesion in the complete optic nerve leads to blindness in that eye.  A lesion in the optic chiasma leads to bitemporal hemianopia.  A lesion in the optic tract leads to homonymous hemianopia.  A lesion in Meyer’s loop leads to homonymous upper quadrantanopia.  Lesion in the optic radiation and visual cortex leads to homonymous hemianopia.  Lesion in the bilateral macular cortex leads to bilateral central scotomas.

questions.question_text: A 23-year-old woman had short stature, webbed neck, low hairline and a broad chest. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: This is caused by a sex chromosome abnormality. The phenotypic females have the genotype of   45X. The features of Turner’s syndrome are low hairline, short stature, broad chest, webbed neck,   and increased carrying angle, failure of breast development and lack of pubic hairs. The IQ level of   these females is either comparable to the general population or lower by a mean of 10 points.

questions.question_text: The risk of certain mental illnesses is increased in first-degree relatives of patients with schizophrenia. However, you can reassure a relative of a patient with one of the conditions described below by stating that there is no increased risk with the following disorder. What is this disorder called?
questions.explanation: In a patient with schizophrenia, there is an increased risk of schizophrenia, schizoaffective disorder   and schizotypal personality disorder in first-degree relatives. In patients with schizoaffective   disorder, the risk of schizophrenia and a mood disorder is increased in first-degree relatives. The risk   of bipolar affective disorder is not increased in first-degree relatives.

questions.question_text: 'If I don't succeed, I must be a complete failure.' Of what thinking error, as described by Beck in his cognitive model, is this an example?
questions.explanation: The patient sees everything in black and white, missing all the shades of grey in between. In   depression, this could lead to the above example.  The others include:  •	Labelling is a global distortion and an overgeneralised negative view of the self. The patient   labels him- or herself as hopeless, incompetent or a victim.  •	Overgeneralisation is predicting a never-ending pattern of loss or defeat from a single event.  •	Selective attention refers to remembering only the negative aspects and focusing selectively on   them.  •	Arbitrary inference is jumping to conclusions without looking at the evidence available

questions.question_text: Which of the following describes a fatal toxicity index?

options.text: Number of cases in which toxic symptoms manifest per million prescriptions issued
Number of cases of fetal or neonatal toxicity due to medication prescribed per million prescriptions issued
Number of overdose deaths per million prescriptions issued
Number of overdose deaths per 10,000 prescriptions issued
Number of overdose deaths per 1000 prescriptions issued

correct_answer.text: Number of overdose deaths per million prescriptions issued

correct_answers.text: Number of overdose deaths per million prescriptions issued

questions.explanation: Fatal toxicity index (FTI) is a measure of the number of overdose deaths per million prescriptions issued. FTI figures suggest high toxicity for tricyclic drugs (especially dosulepin but not lofepramine), medium toxicity for venlafaxine and moclobemide, and low toxicity for selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, mirtazapine and reboxetine.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about gene characteristics is correct?

options.text: A dominant allele, recessive allele, or both can manifest their effects in heterozygotes.
Autosomal dominant disorders do not skip generations
Autosomal recessive disorders do not remain hidden for several generations
Disease genes are described as non-dominant or non-recessive
In X-linked disorders, father-to-son transmission can take place

correct_answer.text: Autosomal dominant disorders do not skip generations

correct_answers.text: Autosomal dominant disorders do not skip generations

questions.explanation: Autosomal dominant disorders do not skip generations. In autosomal recessive disorders, both parents are typically carriers, and the disorders can remain hidden for several generations.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a characteristic feature of Williams' (Williams–Beuren) syndrome?

options.text: Mild learning disability occurs in 75% of the patients
Williams' syndrome is caused by a chromosomal deletion at 7p11.23

correct_answer.text: Mild learning disability occurs in 75% of the patients

correct_answers.text: Mild learning disability occurs in 75% of the patients

questions.explanation: Williams’ syndrome, which is caused by a chromosomal deletion at 7q11.23, presents with   supravalvular aortic stenosis, pulmonary stenosis, mild intellectual disability in around 75% and   unusual facial experience. A prenatal chorionic villous sampling at 10–12 weeks or amniocentesis   at 16–18 weeks of gestation can help in detecting it prenatally. Excessive sociability and   friendliness are present. Williams’ syndrome is characterised by specific neuromorphological and   neurophysiological findings on neuroimaging. MRI shows a proportional sparing of frontal, limbic   and neocerebellar structures. LIM-kinase1 and STX1A are the candidate genes for behavioural and   cognitive function in this syndrome.

questions.question_text: Which nucleus of the thalamus is considered to be a part of the limbic system?
questions.explanation: The anterior nucleus of the thalamus is considered part of the limbic system, playing a role in emotional processing and memory.

questions.question_text: One of your patients was taking an antidepressant medication on her own. She informed you that she purchased this off the market. After some years, she had visual disturbance and was reported to have macular degeneration. Which of the following antidepressants is most likely to cause this?
questions.explanation: St John's wort contains hypericin, which can cause photosensitivity reactions and contribute to macular degeneration.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is the efferent from the cerebellar cortex?
questions.explanation: Purkinje cells are the only efferent (output) neurons from the cerebellar cortex.

questions.question_text: Which of the following are the largest cells of all neurons in the human brain?
questions.explanation: Betz cells are the largest neurons in the human brain, located in the primary motor cortex.

questions.question_text: What is the mechanism of caffeine's neuropsychiatric effects?
questions.explanation: The main action of caffeine is antagonism of adenosine A1- and A2-receptors. Higher doses also   block phosphodiesterase and γ-aminobutyric acid A.

questions.question_text: How much of lithium is present in a 400-mg tablet of lithium carbonate?
questions.explanation: A 400 mg tablet of lithium carbonate contains 10.8 mmol of lithium.

questions.question_text: What is the name of the fraction of individuals with a genotype in whom a disease could manifest?
questions.explanation: Penetrance refers to the proportion of individuals with a particular genotype who exhibit the phenotype associated with that genotype.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a 5-HT2C-receptor antagonist?
questions.explanation: Agomelatine acts as a 5-HT2C-receptor antagonist among its pharmacological actions.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about epigenesis is correct?

options.text: Epigenesis is not an important consideration when behavioural phenotype is considered
Epigenesis refers to processes by which genes are affected by the phenotype
Epigenesis refers to the underlying processes by which the genotype gives rise to a phenotype
Failure of DNA oxidation in fragile X syndrome is an example of a deficit in epigenesis

correct_answer.text: Epigenesis refers to the underlying processes by which the genotype gives rise to a phenotype

correct_answers.text: Epigenesis refers to the underlying processes by which the genotype gives rise to a phenotype

questions.explanation: Epigenesis refers to the underlying processes by which the genotype gives rise to a phenotype.

questions.question_text: For what is sertindole licensed?
questions.explanation: Sertindole is licensed for the treatment of schizophrenia.

questions.question_text: Which immune changes are seen in patients with depression?

options.text: Increased response of lymphocytes to mitogens

questions.explanation: Patients with depression often exhibit lower natural killer cell activity, among other immune changes.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is the correct order in which the genes are expressed to form proteins?

options.text: Modifications of mRNA, transcription, translation and finally post-translational modifications of protein into its mature form
Transcription, modifications of mRNA, translation and finally post-translational modifications of protein into its mature form
Transcription, translation, modifications of mRNA and finally post-translational modifications of protein into its mature form
Translation, modifications of mRNA, transcription and finally transformation of protein into its mature form
Translation, post-translational modifications, transcription and transformation

correct_answer.text: Transcription, modifications of mRNA, translation and finally post-translational modifications of protein into its mature form

correct_answers.text: Transcription, modifications of mRNA, translation and finally post-translational modifications of protein into its mature form

questions.explanation: The correct order is transcription, modifications of mRNA, translation, and finally post-translational modifications of the protein into its mature form.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about fetal alcohol syndrome is correct?

options.text: Drinking 5 units/week is assumed to be safe in the mid to last trimester of pregnancy
Adaptive behaviour is usually well maintained in twins
Concordance rate for monozygotic and dizygotic twins is the same
There is only prenatal growth retardation

questions.explanation: Fetal alcohol syndrome is one of the common preventable causes of learning disability. One   or more drink (one drink = 1.5 oz distilled spirits, 5 oz wine or 12 oz beer) per day in pregnancy   increases the risk of growth retardation, which is both prenatal and postnatal. Characteristic facial   features include dysmorphic facial features (flat philtrum and midface, thin upper lip along with   small palpebral fissures). There is a clear dysfunction of the central nervous system, i.e. behavioural,   neurological and cognitive disabilities. Prevalence of fetal alcohol syndrome is 5.2:10,000 live births.  Monozygotic twins have a concordance rate of 100% whereas it is 60–65% in dizygotic twins.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is useful in the treatment of narcolepsy?
questions.explanation: Narcolepsy is conventionally treated by a low dose of amphetamine and/or monoamine oxidase   inhibitors. Both of these prolong the action of noradrenaline released by the nucleus ceruleus and   reduce rapid eye movement sleep.

questions.question_text: Which of the following neurotransmitters does not activate c-fos?
questions.explanation: C-fos is a protein in the human body, which is encoded by the c-fos gene. It has been measured by   researchers to examine neural activity in the brain. An increase in c-fos messenger RNA in the brain   is indirect indication of increased neural activity. Various stimuli and neuro transmitters can activate   c-fos. g-Aminobutyric acid and glycine do not activate c-fos. Glutamate, dopamine, serotonin,   noradrenaline and adrenaline, acetylcholine, antihistamine and drugs such as amphetamines,   cocaine, haloperidol, morphine and caffeine activate c-fos transcription.

questions.question_text: What is the close pairing of homologous chromosomes during the prophase stage of meiotic division called?
questions.explanation: Synapsis is the process where homologous chromosomes pair closely during prophase I of meiosis, facilitating recombination.

questions.question_text: Which of the following conditions is caused by a trinucleotide (CAG) repeat?
questions.explanation: Huntington's disease is caused by an expanded CAG trinucleotide repeat in the HTT gene.

questions.question_text: Which of the following antidepressants is safe in patients with ventricular arrhythmias?
questions.explanation: Lofepramine is considered safe in patients with ventricular arrhythmias as it lacks significant arrhythmogenic effects.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is the consequence of vitamin B12 deficiency?

options.text: Subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord

correct_answer.text: Subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord

correct_answers.text: Subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord

questions.explanation: Vitamin B12   (cyanocobalamin) deficiency: subacute combined degeneration of spinal cord  Nicotinic acid: pellagra  Thiamine: Wernicke’s encephalopathy  Vitamin E: peripheral and cranial nerve problems.

questions.question_text: Which of the following conditions characterised by severe learning disability, microcephaly and cleft lip is caused by chromosome 13 trisomy?
questions.explanation: Patau's syndrome is caused by trisomy of chromosome 13 and is characterized by severe learning disability, microcephaly, and cleft lip/palate.

questions.question_text: Which of the lysosomal disorders is correctly matched with its corresponding enzyme deficiency?
questions.explanation: Metachromatic leukodystrophy is correctly matched with arylsulphatase A deficiency.

questions.question_text: In relation to schizophrenia, the model of multifocal inheritance assumes that two or more genes at different loci act together, resulting in a clinical phenotype. What is this concept called?
questions.explanation: Epistasis refers to the interaction of multiple genes at different loci contributing to a single clinical phenotype.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a long QTc syndrome?
questions.explanation: Romano–Ward syndrome is an autosomal dominant genetic disorder associated with a prolonged QTc interval and ventricular arrhythmias. Unlike Jervell's and Lange–Nielsen syndromes, it does not include congenital deafness and is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner.

questions.question_text: In which of the following phases of cell cycle does cell division take place?
questions.explanation: Cell division consists of mitosis and meiosis. Many of the somatic cells go through cell division   via the process of mitosis. Mitosis consists of the following stages: (1) interphase, (2) prophase,   (3) metaphase, (4) anaphase and (5) telophase. For replication and nucleic acid synthesis each cell   goes through a natural cycle called the cell cycle. The cell cycle consists of the G1 phase, S phase,   G2 phase and M phase. M phase stands for mitosis phase. Division of the cell takes place in mitosis   phase

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about the Prader–Willi syndrome is correct? note AI chose B

options.text: Compulsive eating is limited to specific foods/eatables/drinks
Compulsive eating is the most disabling behaviour
Hypogonadism is least useful for diagnosis during and after adolescence
It occurs as a result of paternal deletion of 15q11-q21 or maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 15 or an imprinting centre mutation
Self-cutting is the most common form of self-injury found in around 20%

correct_answer.text: Compulsive eating is limited to specific foods/eatables/drinks

correct_answers.text: Compulsive eating is limited to specific foods/eatables/drinks

questions.explanation: In Prader–Willi syndrome, compulsive eating (hyperphagia) is the most disabling behaviour, leading to chronic overeating and obesity. The syndrome results from paternal deletion of 15q11-q21, maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 15, or an imprinting centre mutation.

questions.question_text: With regards to learning disabilities (LDs), which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: Abnormalities of the autosomal chromosomes usually cause no anatomical deformities
Abnormalities of the autosomal chromosomes usually cause mild LDs
Abnormalities of the autosomal chromosomes usually cause severe LDs with widespread anatomical deformities
Abnormalities of the autosomal chromosomes usually cause severe LDs with no anatomical deformities
Sex chromosome abnormalities are always associated with LDs

correct_answer.text: Abnormalities of the autosomal chromosomes usually cause severe LDs with widespread anatomical deformities

correct_answers.text: Abnormalities of the autosomal chromosomes usually cause severe LDs with widespread anatomical deformities

questions.explanation: Abnormalities of the autosomal chromosomes usually cause severe learning disabilities accompanied by widespread anatomical deformities.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is responsible for formation of the hippocampus?
questions.explanation: The dentate gyrus is a part of the hippocampal formation and plays a crucial role in the formation of the hippocampus, which is essential for memory processing.

questions.question_text: A 30-year-old man presented with learning disability, Lisch nodules in the eyes and intracranial tumours. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Von Recklinghausen’s neurofibromatosis: café-au-lait spots, Lisch nodules in the iris, cutaneous   neurofibromas, intracranial tumours and learning disability.  Tuberous sclerosis: shagreen patch, subungual angiomas.  Sturge–Weber syndrome: strawberry naevus, port wine stain, angiomatous malformation of   meningeal vessels, learning disability and epilepsy  Von Hippel-Lindau disease: vascular malformation of retina, hemangioblastoma, pancreatic, adrenal   and renal cysts, and tumours.

questions.question_text: Which of the following describes the differences between variant Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease (vCJD) and sporadic Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease (sCJD)?

options.text: Electroencephalography (EEG) and cerebrospinal fluid examination are more useful in vCJD in sCJD
Tonsillar biopsy is negative in vCJD
Typical EEG changes are seen in vCJD
Variant CJD has an earlier onset of illness than sCJD
Variant CJD is more common than sCJD

correct_answer.text: Variant CJD has an earlier onset of illness than sCJD

correct_answers.text: Variant CJD has an earlier onset of illness than sCJD

questions.explanation: EEG and cerebrospinal fluid examinations are not useful in diagnosing variant CJD. Sporadic CJD is   the more common of the two. The other differences are as shown in Table 5.4

questions.question_text: Which of the following cranial nerves supplies the intrinsic muscles of the tongue?
questions.explanation: The cranial nerve, which supplies trapezius and sternocleidomastoid, is an accessory nerve.   The nerve that supplies the intrinsic muscles of the tongue is the hypoglossal nerve. It is also   responsible for supplying styloglossus, hyoglossus and genioglossus. The cranial nerve supplying   the intrinsic muscles of the larynx is the vagus nerve. It is also responsible for supplying the   constrictor muscles of the pharynx

questions.question_text: Which of the following genetic defects is seen in Down's syndrome?
questions.explanation: This was first described in 1916 in grasshoppers. These translocations in chromosomes were   named after the biologist William Robertson who first described them. Many translocations can   happen across chromosomes but most of these are not compatible with life. The ones that can be   seen in patients are those that involve chromosomes 13, 14, 15, 21 and 22. During robertsonian   translocations (Figure 5.1), the centromeres of two chromosomes fuse and this leads to loss of   the short arms of the chromosomes. Disorders such as Down’s syndrome (trisomy 21) and Patau’s   syndrome (trisomy 13) can occur due to such translocations. The incidence of such translocations is   roughly 1:1000 births.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about Turner's syndrome is correct?

options.text: Imprinted genes affect the brain's structure and function
It is commonly associated with intellectual disability
It is associated with one Barr body
The 'X' chromosome in 'XO' is derived from the mother
The 'X' chromosome in 'XO' is derived from the father

correct_answer.text: Imprinted genes affect the brain's structure and function

correct_answers.text: Imprinted genes affect the brain's structure and function

questions.explanation: From an examination of females with Turner’s syndrome, it can be concluded that the brain   structure and function are affected by the imprinted genes on the sex chromosome. The single   X chromosome can be derived from the maternal or paternal side. If inherited from the maternal   side it affects hippocampal development and if derived paternally it influences the development   of the caudate nucleus and thalamus. Imprinted genes in any imprinting disorders are involved in   cognitive processes. Females with Turner’s syndrome do not have any Barr body. Most females with   Turner’s syndrome have normal intelligence

questions.question_text: Which of the following is the third messenger?
questions.explanation: This acts as a third messenger and can be activated by various second messengers. c-fos has been   identified as an indirect measure of neural activity. Calcium, protein kinase, cAMP, phosphoinositol   and arachidonic acid can act as second messengers. Calcium can also act as the first messenger.   Most serotonin receptors activate a second messenger cascade

questions.question_text: Which of the following cerebral tumours derive from blood vessels?
questions.explanation: Haemangioblastomas are cerebral tumors that derive from blood vessels, specifically the cells involved in blood vessel formation.

questions.question_text: Which of the following structures is part of the occipital lobe?
questions.explanation: The fibres responsible for afferent connections of the hippocampus originate from the cingulate   gyrus, dentate gyrus, indusium griseum, parahippocampal gyrus, secondary olfactory area and   septal nucleus. The occipital lobe consists of primary visual cortex and visual association cortex.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is commonly seen in patients with tardive dyskinesia?

options.text: Increased levels of homovanillic acid in plasma
Presence of lipid peroxidation byproduct in blood

correct_answer.text: Presence of lipid peroxidation byproduct in blood

correct_answers.text: Presence of lipid peroxidation byproduct in blood

questions.explanation: The presence of lipid peroxidation byproducts in the blood is associated with tardive dyskinesia, indicating oxidative stress.

questions.question_text: Which of the following structures contains anterior cingulate cortex?
questions.explanation: The superior mesial region of the frontal lobe contains the anterior cingulate cortex, which is involved in emotion formation and processing, learning, and memory.

questions.question_text: Which of the following features is found in post-stroke patients?
questions.explanation: Pathological crying, also known as emotional incontinence, is commonly found in post-stroke patients due to damage in areas regulating emotional expression.

questions.question_text: Which of these is a method employed to distinguish genetic influence from common environmental effects that contribute to aggregation of disease in families? note AI chose E
questions.explanation: Twin studies are used to distinguish genetic influence from common environmental effects by comparing the concordance rates between monozygotic and dizygotic twins.

questions.question_text: Which of the following tests is used to detect, localise brain lesions and determine their effects?
questions.explanation: Bender’s visual motor gestalt test is a perception test, which is used to evaluate visual and motor   ability through the reproduction of designs. The Halstead–Reitan battery is used to detect and   localise brain lesions and determine their effects. The Luria–Nebraska neuropsychological battery is   used to determine left or right cerebral dominance. It is also used to identify specific types of brain   dysfunction such as dyslexia. The Cambridge neuropsychological test automated battery (CANTAB)   is a sensitive and specific cognitive assessment. The Wechsler’s adult intelligence scale (WAIS) is a   well-standardised test, which gives both verbal and performance IQ

questions.question_text: In which phase of meiosis does recombination take place?
questions.explanation: In prophase 1 of meiosis, there is an alignment and contact of homologous chromosomes pairs.   This allows genetic information to cross over between adjacent chromatids

questions.question_text: Which of the following is consistent with human DNA characteristics?

options.text: It is less than 2 metres long
Total DNA complement in a cell is called a gene
97% of a genome consists of the coding sequence
2–3% of a genome has no apparent function

questions.explanation: The total DNA complement in a cell is called a gene. The total DNA complement in a cell is referred   to as a genome. A human DNA is more than 2 metres long. It contains approximately 3.9 × 10⁹   base-pairs. Only 2–3% of the genome has the coding sequence of approximately 30,000 genes. The   remaining part of the genome has no apparent function.

questions.question_text: In mammalian chromosome replication, approximately what numbers of nucleotides are added per minute?
questions.explanation: During mammalian chromosome replication, approximately 3,000 nucleotides are added per minute.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about Lesch–Nyhan disease is correct?

options.text: Ambivalent statements and coprolalia are characteristic features
It is an autosomal recessive disease
It is an acquired error of purine nucleotide metabolism
Its occurrence in males and females is usually the same
The patients usually have severe intellectual disability

correct_answer.text: Ambivalent statements and coprolalia are characteristic features

correct_answers.text: Ambivalent statements and coprolalia are characteristic features

questions.explanation: Lesch–Nyhan disease is characterized by self-injurious behavior, ambivalent statements, and coprolalia. It is an X-linked recessive disorder, primarily affecting males, and involves a defect in purine nucleotide metabolism.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is related to narcolepsy?
questions.explanation: In animal experiments, it is found that the tuberomammillary nucleus projects widely to the   cerebral cortex and maintains the awake state by activating H1-receptors on cortical neurons.   Orexin receptors are normally present on the histaminergic neurons of the tuberomammillary   nucleus. The key problem is failure of production of the excitatory peptide orexin by a group of   neurons in the lateral hypothalamus.

questions.question_text: Which of the following structures contains a supplementary motor area?
questions.explanation: The superior mesial region of the frontal lobe contains the supplementary motor area, which is involved in the planning and coordination of movement.

questions.question_text: In which of the following is an increased level of homovanillic acid found?
questions.explanation: In schizophrenia, increased levels of homovanillic acid, a dopamine metabolite, are commonly found, reflecting dopaminergic activity.

questions.question_text: Which of the following pairs about dementia and EEG changes is correctly matched?

options.text: Alzheimer's dementia: diffuse slowing of a rhythm
Frontotemporal dementia: focal slow activity in temporal region
Lewy body dementia: increased fast activity wave rhythm
Vascular dementi: initial loss of a waves

correct_answer.text: Alzheimer's dementia: diffuse slowing of a rhythm

correct_answers.text: Alzheimer's dementia: diffuse slowing of a rhythm

questions.explanation: Patients with Alzheimer’s disease tend to show a slowing of α activity. As the disease progresses,   α activity disappears and the EEG is dominated by q and δ activity. The abnormality is mainly   diffuse but in some cases may show predominance over the frontal and temporal lobes. Patients   with frontotemporal dementia usually have a normal EEG. However, the EEG is not a reliable   discriminator between frontotemporal lobe and Alzheimer’s dementia, in either early or late stages.   Patients with Lewy body dementia tend to show greater degree of general slowing and some more   focal slow activity in the temporal region compared with those with Alzheimer’s dementia. Patients   with vascular dementia have α rhythm preserved for longer than those with Alzheimer’s dementia.   In some cases, there may be intermittent slow activity in the temporal lobes. It is not surprising that   patients with pseudodementia have a normal EEG tracing. In Huntington’s disease/dementia there   is low-voltage EEG, initial loss of α waves and later a flattened EEG trace.

questions.question_text: Although nuclear DNA is most important, another cell organelle containing DNA mainly inherited through the female lineage is vital. Which of the following is this cell organelle?
questions.explanation: DNA is mainly contained in the cell nucleus. A tiny amount of DNA is also present in mitochondria.   In a fertilised egg, mitochondria are mainly derived from the mother’s side so inheritance of   mitochondria is mainly through the female lineage. Mitochondrial disorders are usually responsible   for degenerative disorders including ageing. As transmission of mitochondrial DNA is mother to   child, it can be used for genealogical research into an individual’s maternal side.

questions.question_text: To what does a group of conditions that are necessary to provide adequate evidence of a causal relationship between an incidence and a consequence refer?
questions.explanation: These criteria are still widely accepted in the modern era, as a logical structure for investigating and   defining causality in an epidemiological study. The criteria are: consistency, specificity, temporality,   and plausibility, strength of association, biological gradient, coherence, reversibility and analogy

questions.question_text: The association between Alzheimer's disease and Down's syndrome assisted the detection of linkage of familial Alzheimer's disease on chromosome 21. What does this describe?
questions.explanation:
The association between Alzheimer’s disease and Down’s syndrome helps in the detection of   linkage of familial Alzheimer’s disease on chromosome 21, and is known as positional cloning; it is   also sometimes called ‘reverse genetics’. It is a method of gene identification. A gene, the candidate   gene, is identified for a specific phenotype (which will be Down’s syndrome in this case) in the   region (candidate region), and other common traits due to this candidate region. This is followed   by positional cloning which basically involves identification of DNA segments that overlap along   the chromosome towards a candidate gene. The candidate gene approach states that a major component of variation of a phenotype under investigation might be caused by polymorphism of 
the candidate gene.

questions.question_text: At what level is gene expression primarily controlled at? note AI chose D
questions.explanation: Gene expression is primarily controlled at the transcription level, where the DNA is transcribed into messenger RNA (mRNA).

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about Down's syndrome is correct?

options.text: Congenital heart malformations are present in 50% of patients with Down's syndrome
Early deaths are associated with associated congenital anomalies, especially hypothyroidism
In 1960, Down gave the first description of the syndrome now known as Down's syndrome
It was the first syndrome in which a sex-chromosomal anomaly was demonstrated as the basis of characteristic physical features
The underlying genetic abnormality (trisomy 21) was identified in 1980

correct_answer.text: Congenital heart malformations are present in 50% of patients with Down's syndrome

correct_answers.text: Congenital heart malformations are present in 50% of patients with Down's syndrome

questions.explanation: In 1887, Down gave the first description of Down’s syndrome. The underlying genetic abnormality   (trisomy 21) was identified in 1959. Down’s syndrome was the first syndrome in which the typical   physical features were related to a chromosomal anomaly. It accounts for a third of the children   in special education. Life expectancy is less, especially due to the congenital heart malformation.   Hypotonia and short stature are typical. The hypotonia becomes less apparent as the individuals   grow up. Fifteen per cent are hypothyroid by adolescence. Heart malformations are present in   50%. Approximately 7% have congenital upper intestinal obstructions, and 1% have a diagnosis of   leukaemia. Hearing impairment occurs in 60–80% along with visual problems and delayed bone   maturation.

questions.question_text: What is the mutation of a single gene resulting in a disease with a wide range of symptoms called?
questions.explanation: Pleiotropy is from the Greek pleio, which means many, and tropic, which means affecting. Mutation   of a single gene can give rise to a disease with multiple unrelated phenotypes; an example in   humans is phenylketonuria. Mutation of the PAH gene results in reduced/absent activity of   phenylalanine hydroxylase. This can lead to learning difficulties, eczema and pigmentary changes in   the skin.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about dementia in Down's syndrome is correct?

options.text: The e2 allele is associated with an increased risk of dementia
Evidence of dementia is found in 100% of patients after 50 years of age
Frontotemporal dementia is the most common dementia in Down's syndrome
A high risk for dementia in adults with Down's syndrome has been linked to triplication and overexpression of the gene for amyloid precursor protein
There is delayed onset of menopause and dementia in women

correct_answer.text: A high risk for dementia in adults with Down's syndrome has been linked to triplication and overexpression of the gene for amyloid precursor protein

correct_answers.text: A high risk for dementia in adults with Down's syndrome has been linked to triplication and overexpression of the gene for amyloid precursor protein

questions.explanation: There is early onset of menopause and dementia in women with Down’s syndrome. Evidence of   dementia is found in up to half of the patients after age 50. In Down’s syndrome, there is triplication   and overexpression of the gene for amyloid precursor protein (APP). Alzheimer-type dementia is   the most common dementia in patients with Down’s syndrome. The neuropathological changes   are more commonly seen before behavioural manifestations and may be misleading. The e2 allele   is protective; an e4 homozygote is associated with increased risk. In Down’s syndrome, women with   early menopause (46 years of age or younger) were found to have earlier onset and increased risk   of Alzheimer’s disease compared with woman who have their menopause after age 46. It is the   bioavailabili rather than the total estradio that is associated with dementia.

questions.question_text: At which stage of cell division does recombination (also known as crossover) of genetic material occur? AI chose E
questions.explanation: Cross-over of genetic material results in recombination. During the metaphase stage, chromatids   of homologous chromosomes exchange segments by breakage and recombination. Usually,   this happens during meiotic division. It is an important process to maintain genetic diversity.   Sometimes, it can happen in mitotic division in eukaryotes when there is loss of, or damage to, a   segment of chromosome. Recombination helps to repair the genetic material in this situation.

questions.question_text: Velocardiofacial syndrome (VCSF) or Shprintzen's syndrome has an estimated prevalence of 1:3000, i.e. second most common genetic syndrome after Down's syndrome. Which of the following statements about VCSF is correct?

options.text: The 22q11.4 syndrome includes VCSF and DiGeorge's syndrome
It is inherited as an autosomal recessive condition
It is denoted as a 22q11.4 deletion syndrome
Offspring of an individual with deletion of 22q11.2 syndrome have a 50% chance of inheriting the 22q11.2 deletion
The psychotic and affective symptoms emerge only in adulthood

correct_answer.text: Offspring of an individual with deletion of 22q11.2 syndrome have a 50% chance of inheriting the 22q11.2 deletion

correct_answers.text: Offspring of an individual with deletion of 22q11.2 syndrome have a 50% chance of inheriting the 22q11.2 deletion

questions.explanation: This is inherited as autosomal dominant. Approximately a quarter of patients with   velocardiofacial syndrome (VCSF) develop psychotic symptoms. This syndrome is denoted as   22q11.2 deletion syndrome and includes VCSF and DiGeorge’s syndrome. The offspring of an   individual 22q11.2 deletion syndrome have a 50% chance of inheriting the 22q11.2 deletion.   The psychotic and affective symptoms sometimes do emerge in adolescence or early adulthood.   Overall the prevalence of schizophrenia in VCSF is 25 times more than in the general population.   The psychosis associated with VCSF usually runs a chronic course and exhibits a poor response   to antipsychotic treatment. The VCSF is typically characterised by cleft palate (commonest   syndrome associated with cleft palate), cardiac abnormalities and mild learning disabilities. The   patient has a long face with a prominent upper jaw and flattening of his cheeks, and a small   open mouth with an underdeveloped lower jaw. Hypocalcaemia and immunodeficiency are   present. The 22q11 deletion syndrome (22qds) is the second most common human chromosomal   anomaly after Down’s syndrome (trisomy 21) and occurs in approximately in 1: 4,000 births

questions.question_text: Which of the following is an example of chromosomal monosomy?
questions.explanation: Aneuploidy usually arises from failure of pained chromosomes or sister chromatids to disjoin at   anaphase (non-disjunction). Alternatively, aneuploidy may be due to delayed movement of a   chromosome at anaphase (anaphase lag). Thus, by either mechanisms two cells are produced, one   with an extra copy of chromosomes in trisomy and one with them missing in monosomy. The cause   is unknown, but increases in incidence with maternal age.  Polyploidy is the presence of a complete extra set of chromosomes, i.e. 46 + 23 is triploidy with   69 chromosomes and 46 + 46 is tetraploidy with 96 chromosomes. The polyploid cells occur   normally in human bone marrow among megakaryocytes. The tetraploid cells are also a feature of   regenerating livers.

questions.question_text: The 5 mL dose of 509 mg/5 mL oral solution of lithium citrate is equivalent to how many milligrams of lithium carbonate?
questions.explanation: Lithium is available in two preparations: lithium carbonate and lithium citrate. The prophylactic   prescription needs specialist advice. The initiation and change in treatment require more   monitoring. The preparation differs widely in bioavailability.  The lithium content and treatment dosage depend on the preparations; 5 mL lithium citrate   (520 mg/5 mL) is equivalent to 200 mg lithium carbonate

questions.question_text: What is the number of new cases of a disease occurring per year called?
questions.explanation: Incidence refers to the number of new cases of a disease that develop in a specific population during a defined time period.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is correct with regard to catecholamine-O-methyl transferase?

options.text: Affecting the N-methyl-d-aspartate receptor modulator D-serine
Regulating function of dopamine in the frontal cortex

correct_answer.text: Regulating function of dopamine in the frontal cortex

correct_answers.text: Regulating function of dopamine in the frontal cortex

questions.explanation: Dysbindin (DTNBP1) affects glutamate release. Neuregulin (NRG1) plays a role in brain   development, synaptic plasticity and glutamate signalling. COMT is involved in dopamine   regulation in frontal cortex. G72 (DAOA) affects the metabolism of the NMDA-receptor modulator   D-serine. Disrupted in schizophrenia 1 (DISC1) contributes via its role in brain development, cell   functioning and synaptic signalling. PPP3CC has an important role in integration of dopamine and   glutamate signalling

questions.question_text: In which of the following conditions are senile plaques seen?
questions.explanation: Senile plaques are seen in ageing and Down’s syndrome. Neurofibrillary tangles are seen in Down’s   syndrome, ageing, dementia pugilistic (chronic traumatic encephalopathy), Lytico–Bodig disease   (progressive paralysis resembling amyotrophic lateral sclerosis), postencephalitic Parkinson’s   disease, and progressive supranuclear palsy

questions.question_text: From where does an anterior thalamic nucleus receive its efferents?
questions.explanation: Along with the cingulate gyrus, the prefrontal cortex motor cortex, primary auditory cortex and   supplementary motor area supply efferents to the anterior thalamic nucleus, ventral anterior nuclei,   posterior part of ventral lateral thalamic nuclei, medial geniculate body and anterior part of ventral   lateral thalamic nuclei
